rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 and Fig. 2 present the authors' own multitemporal satellite classification of irrigated surface in the Eastern La Mancha groundwater body from 1982 to 2016 (12-14 images per year), and Fig. 3 shows an NDVI time series for a real plot from the authors' SPIDER-ERMOT tool; the paper therefore contains own mapping data, though it is framed mainly as a lessons-learned account.
rows.notes: The paper's material on the governance effect (conflict resolution, water rights allocation, transparency, participation) is narrative: Section 2 states that rights were regularized using the maps with about 95% agreement, but this figure is attributed to a cited reference [2]; it reports the 2012 Supreme Court ruling and the Jury of Irrigation using SPIDER-ERMOT as institutional facts and asserts the tool has 'proven very useful' and that sharing base information is crucial for solving conflicts, without any measured or surveyed result of its own on conflict resolution, transparency or participation. The authors themselves note further research is needed on adequate governance types and on giving legal force to EO-based evidence. Hence Q2 is 'no': the study describes an institutional arrangement rather than reporting its own result on the claimed social-cohesion effect. Q1 is answered 'yes' with some doubt, since the paper is largely descriptive but does include the authors' own mapping time series.

notes: Short conference paper (WIT Transactions 2017) summarising 20 years of remote-sensing-based irrigation mapping in the La Mancha Oriental aquifer and proposing an RS-based water accounting approach; the stated goal of assessing modelled water flows against field data is not actually carried out in the text (no validation data or statistics are presented). Text appears complete.
